fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Two Belief Systems, Not Right and Wrong", "body": "Maryn Green will not frame hospital birth as evil. She frames it as a business running on different beliefs. Her belief is that birth is a natural event, a rite of passage, a process bodies already know how to do because we carry the recipe in our cells, and that babies deserve to be born in peace. The medicalized model believes birth is generally a disaster, that women and babies need saving, and that the process needs controlling. She points out most obstetricians are trained as surgeons and never trained in normal birth, so trouble starts when a woman lands in a setting whose beliefs do not match her own."}, {"title": "The Baby Is a Sovereign Soul", "body": "Green often will not call them babies. She calls them highly evolved souls that happen to be in baby bodies, arriving with their own karmic paths and their own preferences about how and where they want to be born. That reframe moves birth choices away from intellectual decision making toward tuning in, and it lifts blame off mothers when things go sideways. On miscarriage and on births that ignore the plan, she is blunt that we are not responsible for what another soul chooses. Chance Garton connects this to his biofield tuning practice, where he sees challenges a mother carried in pregnancy show up later in her child."}, {"title": "Conception Is Still a Mystery", "body": "Asked what science only pretends to understand, Green starts at conception. An elder taught her that the egg is the creative force and the sperm is the intention, the set of beliefs. She wonders aloud whether conception happens every time given the opportunity, with implantation being the real choice point, and what happens in that week of delay while the father grounds his energy and the soul decides. Garton answers with his own story, a miscarriage last year followed by a dream of an unbreakable little blonde girl, a baby like the one from The Incredibles, on the very day his wife took the positive test."}, {"title": "Informed Choice, Not Informed Consent", "body": "Green corrects the standard phrase. She does not say informed consent because she does not assume anyone will consent and does not need them to. Informed choice means an honest conversation about benefits and risks, after which, she says, most women decline far more than they agree to. As an unlicensed midwife she has no skin in the game and nobody above her requiring routine tests. On ultrasound she stays deliberately unabsolute. Technology is not bad, and peace of mind after a loss has real value, but routine scanning trains a woman to ask someone else whether her baby is okay, which becomes a habit she carries into the birth."}, {"title": "Powerful Women and the Attack on the Family", "body": "Garton noticed that nearly every show he and his wife watched during their first pregnancy carried something horrific about mothers or babies, and calls it deliberate fear programming. Green agrees and goes further. Scaring women and convincing them they are broken keeps them from a power that would change the world, and birth is where that power gets seized away from the family. She describes surrender at the gate, going to the stars to get your baby, her near painless ninth birth of Cove River and her excruciating tenth, and giving her license back."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Maryn Green of the Indie Birth Association joins InnerVerse to discuss her private midwifery practice and experience as a guide to sacred birth. We talk about the intuitive knowledge within the female body, biofield consequences of pregnancy and birth, what "the science" still doesn't know about the creation of life, miscarriage support, old wives tales, ultrasound imaging, practicing informed medical choice, what we see as a cultural conspiracy to scare women about having children, and the mystical non-sedated birth.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension we discuss the spiritual and biological significance of the placenta, hospital harvesting of birth materials, the divine twin symbolism, the potentials of placentophagy, the secret transmission of ancestral wisdom, issues with state-licensed midwifery and why Maryn gave hers back, utilizing the power of Private Member Associations, life after birth and mothering the mother.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The Birth After the Birth", "body": "Maryn Green opens the second hour on the organ most mothers never hear about. Her own first placenta, in a hospital, was one she never even saw, and she has since come to revere an organ the body grows from scratch, with a fetal side and a maternal side and a pathway of communication between mother and baby that she doubts biology fully explains. She teaches women during pregnancy that they are not done when the baby arrives, so that afterward they simply ask for a bowl and birth the placenta themselves, and the whole room can feel the moment the birth is complete."}, {"title": "Ark, Egg, Lotus and Divine Twin", "body": "Chance Garton reads the placenta into cosmogony. Creation stories, he argues, are usually recreations, so the ark opening after a flood and the cracking of the cosmic egg are one image, and in the microcosm that vessel may be the placenta, perhaps even a guardian angel or divine twin. Maryn answers with lotus birth, where the cord is left uncut for days and the placenta preserved with herbs and salt, and with midwives' reports that babies often cry when the cord is severed. Chance notes that creator gods like Brahma emerge from a lotus, and that the Greek root of placenta means cake."}, {"title": "Honoring What Hospitals Call Waste", "body": "Much of the hour is about respect for an organ hospitals treat as waste. Maryn describes the placenta tour she offers families a few hours after birth, showing its puzzle-like maternal side, the amniotic sac the baby just left, and the fetal side whose vessels branch like a tree of life. She never rushes cutting the cord and has left many a scissor at someone's house so parents can decide the moment themselves. Families later make prints, tinctures or a burial ceremony. Chance adds his audience's idea that ancestral memory passes through the placenta, and Maryn mocks cord banking as selling the baby's own blood back to the parents."}, {"title": "The License and Where Loyalty Goes", "body": "Chance frames a license as state permission to do what one otherwise has no right to do, then asks why Maryn returned hers. She apprenticed under an unlicensed Chicago midwife whose house was searched and who received cease and desist orders, then under a fully licensed midwife in Arizona, and assumed her own license would make her safer and more legitimate. Two years of conflict with Arizona taught her otherwise: her loyalty was expected to sit with a medicalized board writing rules about midwifery without understanding it. Chance describes the recited scripts at his Missouri birth center, and Maryn asks how anyone can offer autonomy without having it."}, {"title": "A Private Association Practiced in the Open", "body": "Chance says private membership associations came onto his radar during the lockdown years, but Maryn had been using one for about thirteen years. She returned her Arizona license with a defiant letter, to the annoyance of her lawyers, then found a book on the old association model whose author lived twenty minutes away. To her knowledge she was the first midwife in the country to work this way, and she practiced openly in Sedona without ever hearing from the state. She insists it is no magic bullet, only the outer form of continuous inner work. Chance closes by linking the names Margot and Maryn to the sea mother archetype."}]

fields.Plus Quotes JSON: [{"text": "I think essentially to me, the placenta just represents life, in a really profound way.", "author": "Maryn Green", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/960b3120-9137-43a8-80de-ab003f52c451/MARYN-GREEN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "I think that honoring the placenta is much more important than is really widely recognized.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "I didn't know that my loyalty was going to have to be placed with the state, which is the medical system.", "author": "Maryn Green", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/960b3120-9137-43a8-80de-ab003f52c451/MARYN-GREEN.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "We're paying them to serve us, not for us to be subservient to them.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "How can you offer autonomy to people when you are not autonomous, when you have someone looking over your shoulder?
